result: Prior work (Santos-Lopez et al., 2019) established that selection of A. baumannii in biofilm versus planktonic environments with ciprofloxacin produced distinct genotypes and phenotypes, with biofilm-selected populations showing lower ciprofloxacin resistance and collateral sensitivity to β-lactam drugs.
evaluation: Claims C1-C3 are all supported by citation to the same prior work (Santos-Lopez et al., 2019) and establish the historical context for the current study. These claims describe prior work rather than current findings and are appropriately attributed.

result: After 3 days of subinhibitory CAZ selection, history was the dominant force explaining 61.7% of phenotypic variation in resistance, with selection contributing 30.7% and chance only 7.6%. All populations showed significant increases in CAZ resistance at this timepoint.
evaluation: Claims C26-C28 and C74 are supported by statistical analysis (nested ANOVA with p-values reported) and experimental data shown in Figure 2. The variance partitioning methodology is described and appropriate for the experimental design. The claim that all populations increased resistance is statistically supported (p=0.0080).

result: By day 12 of CAZ treatment at 4× MIC, selection became the dominant force (47.8% of variation) while history's contribution decreased to 31.4%, indicating that strong selective pressure can diminish but not erase historical effects. All populations showed significant resistance increases.
evaluation: Claims C29-C31 and C75 are supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 2 with appropriate p-values (p≤0.0001). The temporal shift in variance contributions from history-dominated to selection-dominated is clearly demonstrated. The inference that strong selection diminishes historical effects (C31) is appropriately drawn from the quantitative data.

result: Populations with lower initial CAZ MICs increased resistance more than those with higher initial MICs, showing a diminishing returns pattern. More resistant populations did not increase resistance further, while susceptible populations rapidly compensated.
evaluation: Claims C32 and C82 are supported by correlation analysis (Spearman r = -0.84, p=0.044 at day 12) shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1. The negative correlation at day 12 supports the diminishing returns interpretation. Claims C68-C69 appropriately summarize this pattern, though they are somewhat redundant with C32.

result: During IMI selection, no overall resistance change occurred at day 3 (subinhibitory concentrations), but significant increases occurred by day 12 at 4× MIC. More sensitive populations gained more resistance than less sensitive ones at day 3, showing negative correlation with initial MIC.
evaluation: Claims C40-C41 and C76 are supported by statistical analysis (nested ANOVA, p=0.3524 for day 3, p<0.0001 for day 12) shown in Figure 2. Claim C42 is supported by data in Figure 2C and supplement. Claim C83 provides correlation statistics (Spearman r = -0.9258, p=0.033 at day 3) supporting the pattern.

result: For IMI resistance evolution, selection explained 43.1% of phenotypic variation while history explained 33.2%.
evaluation: Claim C43 is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 2 with significance indicated (p<0.05). The variance partitioning is consistent with the methodology described and appropriately quantifies the relative contributions of evolutionary forces.

result: After 12 days of CAZ selection, the grand mean of CIP resistance did not change overall, but biofilm-derived populations became significantly more sensitive to CIP while planktonic-derived populations did not, demonstrating that collateral sensitivity emergence depends on prior selection environment.
evaluation: Claims C35-C36 are supported by experimental data in Figure 3A showing differential responses between B and P populations. The inference in C37 that collateral sensitivity depends on prior environment is appropriately drawn from the differential responses observed. However, statistical tests for the B vs P comparison are not explicitly reported in the text.

result: All 12 populations evolved in CAZ became more resistant to IMI, with selection explaining 44.3% of variation, history 23.0%, and chance 32.2%, demonstrating cross-resistance between these β-lactam antibiotics.
evaluation: Claims C38-C39 are well-supported by statistical analysis (nested t-test p<0.0001, t=7.507, df=34) and variance partitioning shown in Figure 3E. The cross-resistance pattern is clearly demonstrated with appropriate statistical rigor.

result: Evolution in IMI did not affect CIP resistance on average (history explained 75% of variation), but produced collateral sensitivity to CIP in two biofilm-derived populations.
evaluation: Claims C44-C45 are supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C and 3F. The dominance of history (75%) is clearly shown. However, the claim of collateral sensitivity in "two B populations" should be verified against the figure data to ensure accurate counting.

result: Selection in CAZ increased IMI resistance, but selection in IMI did not increase CAZ resistance, revealing an asymmetry in cross-resistance between these drugs.
evaluation: Claim C46 is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3B and 3D, which clearly demonstrate the asymmetric cross-resistance pattern. This is an important finding that distinguishes the mechanisms of resistance to these two β-lactam antibiotics.

result: At the genotypic level, evolution in CAZ was shaped more by selection than history, while the opposite pattern was seen in IMI, with similar effects of chance in both experiments.
evaluation: Claims C47-C48 are supported by genomic analysis using Manhattan distance metrics shown in Figure 4. The methodology for calculating genotypic contributions of evolutionary forces is described in detail in the Materials and Methods. The contrasting patterns between CAZ and IMI are clearly demonstrated.

result: During the history phase, biofilm lines selected mutations in adeL (regulator of adeFGH pump) producing collateral sensitivity to β-lactams, while planktonic lines selected adeN or pgpB mutations conferring cross-resistance to CAZ.
evaluation: Claims C50-C51 are supported by genomic data shown in Figure 1D and citation to prior work (Santos-Lopez et al., 2019). This establishes the mechanistic basis for the differential evolutionary trajectories observed in the selection phase.

result: Evolution in CAZ selected at least one mutation in adeJ (encoding the permease subunit of AdeIJK efflux pump) in 16 of 18 populations, a known cause of CAZ resistance in clinical isolates.
evaluation: Claim C52 is supported by genomic sequencing data shown in Figure 4A with clear quantification (16/18 populations). Claim C53 is supported by citation to Lee et al., 2017 and represents established knowledge about the function of adeJ in CAZ resistance.

result: Evolution in IMI selected mutations in ftsI (encoding penicillin binding-protein 2) in all populations, one of the most common causes of de novo IMI resistance in clinical isolates.
evaluation: Claim C54 is supported by genomic sequencing data shown in Figure 4B demonstrating 100% penetrance. Claim C55 is supported by citation to Lee et al., 2017 and represents established knowledge about ftsI's role in IMI resistance.

result: Evolution in β-lactam antibiotics generated convergent evolution at the genetic level regardless of genetic background.
evaluation: Claim C56 is supported by the high frequency of mutations in the same genes (adeJ for CAZ, ftsI for IMI) across populations with different ancestral backgrounds, as shown in Figure 4. The inference is appropriately supported by citations to similar findings in other studies.

result: Five replicate IMI populations that acquired the same mutation in ftsI (A579V) differed in resistance levels by up to fourfold, suggesting that genetic background or additional mutations influence phenotype.
evaluation: Claim C57 is supported by genomic and phenotypic data shown in Figure 4 and source data. This demonstrates that identical mutations can produce different phenotypes depending on genetic context, though the authors acknowledge that follow-up experiments are needed to definitively test this hypothesis.

result: Genetic reversions of adeL mutations occurred five times in CAZ lines and three times in IMI lines, and these back-mutations reversed resistance tradeoffs between β-lactams and CIP.
evaluation: Claims C58-C60 are supported by genomic sequencing data shown in Figure 4A-B and phenotypic data in Figure 3. The frequency of reversions is clearly quantified. The connection between reversions and phenotypic changes is demonstrated by comparing genomic and phenotypic data across figures.

result: Genetic reversion of parC mutations occurred in each P3 replicate propagated in CAZ.
evaluation: Claim C61 is supported by genomic sequencing data shown in Figure 4A. The authors also conducted a follow-up experiment (Figure 4—figure supplement 1) to confirm that the reversion arose de novo rather than from standing variation, strengthening this result.

result: The high frequency of mutational reversions indicates that resistance determinants selected during the history phase are under enormous constraint and impose fitness costs in the presence of CAZ or IMI.
evaluation: Claim C64 is an inference supported by the observed frequency of reversions (C58-C61) and citation to Pennings et al., 2021. The logic is sound: reversions would only be selected if the original mutations impose fitness costs in the new selective environment. However, direct fitness measurements would strengthen this conclusion.

result: Selection is the predominant force in AMR evolution and produces convergent evolution, but history and chance play important roles in the emergence of resistance phenotypes, extent of resistance, collateral sensitivity networks, and predictability of final phenotypes.
evaluation: Claims C65-C66 appropriately synthesize the major findings from the variance partitioning analyses (Figures 2-4) and are supported by the experimental data throughout the manuscript. The nuanced conclusion that selection dominates but does not eliminate effects of history and chance is well-supported.

result: Evolution of AMR follows a diminishing returns pattern, where antibiotic pressure selects for mutations with progressively smaller phenotypic effects as populations are treated with higher antibiotic concentrations.
evaluation: Claim C67 is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 demonstrating negative correlations between initial MIC and resistance gains. This pattern is consistent with established evolutionary theory and similar findings in other systems.

result: Strong selection in new drugs reduced but did not erase historical effects, revealing important contingencies. A history of biofilm selection constrained resistance to new drugs and led to frequent genetic reversions rather than compensatory mutations, creating potential vulnerabilities to orthogonal drugs.
evaluation: These claims synthesize the main findings of the study and are supported by the variance partitioning analyses (showing reduced but persistent historical effects), the reversion data (C58-C61), and the collateral sensitivity patterns (C36-C37, C45). The claims appropriately integrate phenotypic and genotypic data.

result: The manuscript reviews established evolutionary theory and prior work on the roles of history, chance, and selection in evolution, including specific applications to antibiotic resistance evolution.
evaluation: Claims C8-C22 are all supported by appropriate citations to prior work and represent established knowledge in evolutionary biology and AMR research. These claims provide necessary background context for the current study.

result: Acinetobacter baumannii is a leading agent of multidrug-resistant infections worldwide and is named as an urgent threat by the CDC.
evaluation: Claims C23-C24 are supported by citation to CDC, 2019 and represent established public health knowledge about the clinical importance of A. baumannii.

result: The level of evolved resistance converges and may be predictable, though effects of genetic background remain.
evaluation: Claim C33 is inferred from the diminishing returns pattern (C32, C67) and supported by citations, but the predictability aspect is speculative. The data show convergence in some aspects (genetic parallelism) but persistent divergence in others (phenotypic variation despite same mutations). The claim is appropriately hedged with "may be" but requires further work to definitively establish predictability.

result: The manuscript cites established knowledge about resistance mechanisms in clinical isolates and the effects of genetic background on resistance evolution.
evaluation: Claims C49, C62-C63, C70-C72 are all supported by appropriate citations to prior work and represent established knowledge relevant to interpreting the current findings.

result: The experimental timescale (160 generations over 12 days) is clinically relevant and the antibiotic concentrations used (up to 4× MIC) are appropriate for studying resistance evolution.
evaluation: Claim C73 is supported by citation to Gibson et al., 2018 providing context for the clinical relevance of the timescale. Claim C77 is supported by citation to Nightingale, 1980 regarding maximum killing at 4× MIC. These claims justify the experimental design choices.

result: The manuscript reports key methodological details including population sizes (4.7×10^8 CFU/mL at day 1, 2.8×10^9 at day 12), sequencing coverage (mean 358× ± 106), and detection of standing genetic variation in clone B2.
evaluation: Claims C78-C81 report methodological details that are appropriately documented. These are important for assessing the adequacy of population sizes for detecting mutations and the quality of genomic data. The detection of standing variation in B2 (C81) is relevant for interpreting some results.
